Innerdance Biofeedback — Concept for Medical Review

Document type: Platform description for medical and scientific reviewers, and new team members — what the system collects, computes, and reports. It does not cover the project's research objective or hypotheses; see the companion objectives & hypotheses document (internal) for that. Version: 3 — split into a platform description (this doc) and a separate objectives/hypotheses doc Status: Proof-of-concept · exploratory · not yet validated for clinical use

The one-sentence pitch

A system that measures how a person's nervous system responds to sound in real time, then tracks that response against a personal baseline over weeks — using both signals to personalise the sound and reveal lasting change in autonomic resilience and flexibility.

This document describes that system: how session data is collected, cleaned, turned into HRV metrics — the platform that enables data collection, hypothesis generation, and hypothesis testing. For why we're building it and what we hypothesise it will show, see the companion objectives & hypotheses document (internal).

What the system does

A participant wears a standard chest-strap heart-rate monitor (Polar H10, ~€100), recording continuously across three phases: a pre-session resting baseline, the session itself, and a post-session resting baseline. The system then:

  1. Measures how the autonomic nervous system responded to each stage of the music
  2. Compares the response to the participant's own baseline (see Choice of metrics — first version below)
  3. Explains what happened in plain language — for participant, facilitator, and reviewer

No invasive sensors are used, and every interpretive rule is cited to its source publication.

What's actually built, today

  • Sound + ECG DB — raw recordings stored: playlist audio and each participant's uploaded ECG/RR data
  • Data pipeline — cleans the recording and computes HRV + acoustic features from it (see Data pipeline below)
  • Processed data DB — the computed metrics, stored per session
  • User report UI — the participant-facing HTML report shown in Examples from real session data below

What might the system do in the future

The diagram above sketches the full intended architecture — most of it does not exist yet. In this envisioned end state:

User Would see Would contribute
Participant A personal report: high/low points reached, against a normal or innerdance-population reference ECG recording, self-report
Facilitator How each stage affected the group; which sound features drove which response Facilitation notes, expert validation
Medical practitioner Participant data; an acoustic-features-vs-stage heat map Clinical interpretation, guidance on meaningful signals
Developer / Analyst Full pipeline, notebooks, model training, dashboards New features, model refinements, protocol design

Beyond today's measure/compare/explain, possible future capabilities include learning which acoustic features drove which physiological responses, in whom, and recommending adjustments to the sound or session design to optimise the outcome.

Choice of metrics — first version

Metric Valid when Role
SD2 Any breathing rate Primary — stage-wise, longitudinal, and multi-participant comparisons
DFA α1 Breathing rate > 9 bpm Primary — fractal complexity of the heartbeat (≈1.0 healthy; <0.75 more disorganised; >1.4 overly regular)
RMSSD Most reliable at rest (pre/post baseline) Computed throughout, but only read with confidence at pre/post baseline
SD1/SD2 Breathing rate confirmed Short- vs long-term variability balance
Heart rate / breathing rate Any condition / estimated from the HRV signal Context and validity checks

All metrics are computed from validated, open-source implementations, cross-checked against the peer-reviewed literature (see References). SDNN, used in early per-session reports, has since been dropped in favor of SD2 alone, which behaves more consistently over the shorter, non-resting windows used inside a session.

This is a sample set, not a fixed one. These are the metrics we currently compute and report on; we expect the set to evolve as the hypotheses being tested change — new metrics may be added, and current ones may turn out not to be the right fit.

Examples from real session data

1. Per-session report. From the actual HTML report generated for a participant: metrics across the 12 stages, and the same stages' acoustic profile that produced them.

2. Session comparison. Across a participant's repeated sessions: resting RMSSD/SD2/DFA α1 pre vs post, the resilience arc (Stage 10 − Stage 4), and recovery % — the same metrics tracked in chronological order, which is what lets us eventually ask whether a person's baseline shifts over weeks, not just within one session.

Data pipeline

This is the pipeline structure we plan to build, so that a participant's report, a dashboard query, and a research analysis all start from identical numbers: clean & load the raw recording → merge with session metadata → filter to usable windows → compute metrics → derive additional features → data-quality gate → baseline/session plots → interpretation → medical validation.

So far we do not have the data-quality gate, interpretation, or medical validation steps — filter criteria are still being decided, and everything from the data-quality gate onward does not exist yet. Raw recordings and computed metrics are each saved, not just the final chart, so any step can be re-derived without re-running everything from scratch.

Rules vs. models vs. adaptive personalisation

This classification approach is Phase 0 of a longer roadmap, not the end state. We are prototyping with deterministic rules deliberately — every classification is traceable to a specific metric crossing a specific threshold from a specific paper, with no black-box inference — and intend to scale toward data-driven phases once enough per-participant and cross-participant data exists (see the project plan in the companion objectives & hypotheses document (internal)).

Phase Approach
0 — now Deterministic rules with literature-cited thresholds
1 Within-person models: how each individual's ANS responds to specific acoustic features
2 Cross-participant models: pool information across individuals while preserving individual differences — important given resting HRV can vary 5–10× between people
3+ Adaptive personalisation: the system gradually learns which acoustic interventions work for which participant profiles, validated prospectively before any deployment

Model type and validation approach for Phases 1–3+ will be defined with domain, statistical, and medical advisors — not fixed in advance.

What we have built so far

These components are up and running, and all of them are expected to keep changing as the approach is iterated on:

  • HRV processing pipeline (hrv_core.py)
  • Acoustic feature extraction (acoustic_core.py)
  • Interpretive rule engine (hrv_rules.py) — draft; not yet wired into report generation, and awaiting medical review
  • Per-session report, longitudinal trend view (examples above)
  • Database (Supabase)
  • React upload UI — handles ECG upload + playback sync

Not yet started: data-quality gate, model/training layer.

Known limitations and gaps

  • RMSSD is only reliably interpretable at rest with stable breathing (McCreary et al. 2022) — it is still computed in-session but should be read with caution there.
  • The "filter to valid windows" and "data quality gate" pipeline steps are not yet formal, enforced checks.
  • DFA α1's scale range was corrected in June 2026 (4–16 → 4–12 beats, matching neurokit2 to <0.002); historical figures should be checked for which scale they used.

For limitations affecting how much the hypotheses (not the pipeline) can currently support — sample size, causal claims — see the companion objectives & hypotheses document (internal).
